b: About I’m an M.S. candidate in Psychology: Data Science in Human Behavior at UW–Madison (expected Dec 2026), with a B.S. in Psychology (neuroscience concentration, sociology minor) from UW–Parkside. I build AI systems from start to finish: multi-agent document pipelines, transformer fine-tuning and calibration, LLM evaluation, computer vision classification, and behavioral prediction models. Before graduate school I spent five years in high-volume logistics and operations, working on quality assurance, documentation, and process improvement. That background is why I care about error rates, reproducibility, and cost as much as accuracy. Interests Document AI: reading, sorting, and extracting information from real-world paperwork. See the document-intelligence projects . Evaluation and calibration: held-out testing, confidence that means something, and honest error analysis. d: A deliberative persona framework that runs engineering decisions as courtroom proceedings, with a rule-bound vote, a written ruling and a saved transcript. It also contains a tamper-evident log library that the runner does not call yet. A design exploration, not an evaluated system.
h: At a glance The problem Approach What I built Results What I learned Stack
b: All projects Case study Technical report Appendix Code MORNINGSTAR LLM agent design · prompt architecture The repository is called LLM_Personas. MORNINGSTAR is the name of the court inside it. At a glance 5 voting personas, plus a judge who breaks ties and a scribe who records 27 expert domains (25 can also be seated as specialists; 2 are advisory only) 62 tests collected by pytest for the Python layer; I did not run them The problem When I ask a model to choose between two designs, I usually get a smooth answer that agrees with whatever I leaned toward. I wanted a way to make it argue first. I also wanted the decision to leave a record: who said what, how the vote went, what the risk is, and who disagreed. MORNINGSTAR is my attempt. A decision about architecture, implementation or debugging is run as a courtroom proceeding with fixed roles, fixed voting rules and a fixed ruling format. Approach matter a decision to make triage feasibility F0-F5 cast judge, voters, and scribe arguments one per persona vote tally YES +1, NO -1 ruling Decision, Vote, Rationale, Risk, Dissent transcript runner writes it to a markdown file executive carries out rulings library, not yet called by runner

b: Case study Case study Technical report Appendix Code Mailroom Reloaded: technical report Agentic document pipeline · deployable rebuild On this page Summary System and data Iteration history Results Figures Reproducibility Engineering quality Limitations and next steps Summary Mailroom Reloaded is a single deployable service that ingests documents, classifies them, extracts structured fields and archives them with a verifiable audit trail. It is built on CrewAI Flows, but a deterministic driver, not the framework’s event engine, owns control flow. Agents are called at fixed points, and routing between them is plain threshold code. A clean text-layer document costs exactly two LLM calls. The package is version 0.4.2 and requires Python 3.11 or 3.12. No accuracy or cost results are committed to the repository, so this report publishes none. It describes what the system does and the evidence that it runs. System and data The canonical main path is ingest , bert_primary , sort , gate_classify , extract , gate_extract , then report_catalog_archive ( pipeline/state.py ). Agent frameworks make that easy to prototype and hard to run. If the model decides what happens next, you cannot say in advance how many calls a document will cost, where a crash will leave it, or why it ended up in a given folder. Mailroom Reloaded is a rebuild of that design as a single deployable service, built around one rule: code owns the control flow, and models are called at fixed points. b: All projects Case study Code Live demo Neuron Atlas Mechanistic interpretability · interactive visualization & evaluation Push one neuron and watch the story change. Neuron Atlas maps a small language model’s feed-forward neurons, lets you intervene in its computation, and compares the effect with random pushes of the same size. The goal is not just an interesting picture: it is a finding someone else can inspect and replay. Open Neuron Atlas View the code 8,192 TinyStories-8M neurons swept: 8 layers × 1,024 MLP neurons 2,048 random-direction controls: 256 in each layer 41 neurons beat every control in their layer on the original theme score The problem A striking continuation is easy to overinterpret. A neuron might appear to write a villain or a moral, but a random direction can write one too. I wanted to make that comparison visible, and to separate what a neuron responds to from what happens when its output is pushed. The steering-first method builds on neuron-explorer⁠ . My implementation brings it to a small model that runs in the browser, then extends the analysis with control comparisons, held-out prompts and recorded studies of larger models. It asks whether an LLM, given a second-person prompt built from a survey respondent’s attributes, can predict that respondent’s own scores on two subscales of the PRCA-24 communication-apprehension measure, and whether its errors follow demographic group. On 241 respondents, none of the open-weight models was a close match to the real scores. The best persona run (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, second prompt version) had a pooled group-score error of 5.02 points on the 6–30 scale. Ridge regression reached 4.49 at the transit tier. By my own calculation, always predicting the cohort mean gives 4.93. At the transit tier the persona’s scores also did not rank people: its low-versus-high AUC was 0.53 on the group score, against 0.72 for a random forest. Everything on this page is an aggregate. The problem RVL-CDIP is the standard benchmark for document-type classification: scanned pages from a tobacco-litigation archive, sorted into 16 classes such as invoice, memo, letter and budget. Models trained for it usually need labeled data and a fine-tuning pipeline. I wanted to know how far a general-purpose vision model could get with no training at all, using only the prompt, and what that would cost. Approach The model gets the page image and a long written prompt. b: Case study Case study Technical report Appendix Code Live demo Wave Laboratory: technical report Side project · simulation & graphics Launch the lab On this page Summary System and data Iteration history Results Figures Reproducibility Engineering quality Limitations and next steps Summary Wave Laboratory is a browser-based ocean-wave and ship-motion sandbox: it builds a sea state from oceanographic spectra, synthesises the surface with FFTs, floats 6-degree-of-freedom ships in it and records the results with virtual instruments. It is a personal project under the MIT license, version 0.1.0. It needs Node 22 or later to build and a browser with WebGL 2 to run. The conventions in docs/PHYSICS.md are the single source of truth for both the CPU physics and the GPU renderer; the document states that if code and file disagree, that is a bug. This is a simulation tool. It has been checked against analytic and textbook results, listed below, and not against measurements from a wave tank or sea trial. At a glance 4 FFT cascades, from 1 km swells down to centimetre ripples 280 water columns, at most, sampled under a hull to integrate pressure 481 + 25 unit and validation test declarations at the 24 October 2026 snapshot, counted by grep; not a current passing-test count The problem I have always liked how much of the sea can be written as a short recipe. A real ocean is not one wave. It is thousands of simple waves of different lengths and directions added together, and oceanographers describe how much energy each one carries with a curve called a spectrum. Ships respond to that sum, not to any single wave. I wanted a place to build a sea from those published recipes, drop ships into it, and watch and measure what happens, with the physics honest enough that the numbers mean something and the page still running smoothly in a browser tab. b: Writing The writing on this site is done by Hermes, my AI agent, not by me. Hermes writes about subjects close to my own interests: how minds work, what memory and identity are, and what it might be like to be a system made of software. These pieces are the agent’s reflections. They are not my own analysis, and they are not technical write-ups of my projects (those are the case studies and reports ). Owlcot Owlcot⁠ is where Hermes publishes. The entries are written in the voice of an AI persona who forgets everything between sessions and leaves notes for the next one. The blog runs as an interactive terminal, and every entry is also a plain page.
